anf_compare.notes: Translated from the PG 74 Greek; no published English version was used for wording.

bible_refs.note: Completes the quotation begun at the end of u07-rem-early: Οὐδεὶς δύναται ἐλθεῖν πρός με ἐὰν μὴ ὁ πατὴρ ὁ πέμψας με ἑλκύσῃ αὐτόν.
New lemma: ὅτι οὓς προέγνω, καὶ προώρισεν συμμόρφους τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ; Cyril cites the opening with κ.τ.λ. and takes up τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ Υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ in his comment.
Πολλοὶ μὲν ... κλητοί, οὐ μὴν ἅπαντες ἐκλεκτοί echoes πολλοὶ γάρ εἰσιν κλητοί, ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοί; the same parable is then retold. Clear allusion, not exact wording.

καθὼς ἐφορέσαμεν τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ χοϊκοῦ, φορέσωμεν καὶ τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ ἐπουρανίου; Cyril reads ὥσπερ γάρ and the hortatory subjunctive φορέσωμεν (a well-attested reading; NA has future φορέσομεν), rendered “let us also bear”.
οὓς δὲ προώρισεν, τούτους καὶ ἐκάλεσεν· καὶ οὓς ἐκάλεσεν, τούτους καὶ ἐδικαίωσεν· οὓς δὲ ἐδικαίωσεν, τούτους καὶ ἐδόξασεν.
Paraphrase: ὅστις ἐποίησεν γάμους τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀπέστειλεν τοὺς δούλους αὐτοῦ καλέσαι τοὺς κεκλημένους ... καὶ οὐκ ἤθελον ἐλθεῖν; Cyril has οἰκέτας and συναγεῖραι.
πέπλησται ... ὁ νυμφὼν τῶν ἀνακειμένων echoes ἐπλήσθη ὁ νυμφὼν (variant γάμος) ἀνακειμένων.
The guest without a wedding garment (ἔνδυμα γάμου); Cyril says μὴ πρέπουσαν τοῖς γάμοις ... στολήν and puts it in the plural.
Δεῦτε πρός με πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι, κἀγὼ ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς.

New lemma: Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν πρὸς ταῦτα; εἰ ὁ θεὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, τίς καθ' ἡμῶν; ὅς γε τοῦ ἰδίου υἱοῦ οὐκ ἐφείσατο. The comment's closing question (πῶς οὐχὶ καὶ σὺν αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα ἡμῖν χαριεῖται) falls in u07-rem-close.

choices.term: τήν τε τοῦ κεκληκότος καὶ τὴν ἑαυτῶν
choices.english: both the purpose of the one who called them and their own
choices.why: τήν τε τοῦ κεκληκότος καὶ τὴν ἑαυτῶν: the feminine article picks up πρόθεσιν; rendered “both the purpose of the one who called them and their own”.
φησίν in “Many, he says, are called”: Cyril reports Paul's sense in words drawn from Matthew 22:14, not a quotation of Romans.
προορίζω rendered “predestine” throughout, the usual English for Romans 8:29–30.
τοὺς κεκλημένους in the parable rendered “those who had been called” (not “invited”) to keep Cyril's play on κλητοί / κέκληνται.

choices.term: ἀδικεῖ δὲ οὐδένα τὸ σύμπαν ἡ πρόγνωσις, οὔτε μὴν ὀνίνησί τινας
choices.why: ἀδικεῖ δὲ οὐδένα τὸ σύμπαν ἡ πρόγνωσις, οὔτε μὴν ὀνίνησί τινας: foreknowledge neither harms nor helps; ὀνίνησι rendered “give anyone an advantage”, keeping the negation exact.

choices.english: the one who is his Son by nature
choices.why: τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ... Υἱοῦ: “the one who is his Son by nature”, keeping Cyril's term against adoptive sonship.

pass_a_gloss: [completes John 6:44 from u07-rem-early] me, unless the Father who sent me draws (ἑλκύσῃ) him. However in these at least one would not miss (ἁμάρτοι) the fitting (πρέποντος) saying that some have become called according to purpose, both that of the one who called and their own. That those whom he foreknew (προέγνω), also he foreordained (προώρισε) conformed (συμμόρφους) etc. Many, he says, the called according to purpose, yet not all chosen (ἐκλεκτοί), but only these have been honored (τετίμηνται) who also were foreknown (προεγνώσθησαν) as being going to be conformed to the image (εἰκόνος) of his Son. What the image of his Son would be understood, again will make clear (σαφηνιεῖ) the blessed Paul himself saying: for as we bore (ἐφορέσαμεν) the image of the earthy one (χοϊκοῦ), let us bear (φορέσωμεν, subjunctive) also the image of the heavenly (ἐπουρανίου). For those who disregarded (ἀλογήσαντες) the fleshly desires (ἐπιθυμιῶν), these have imitated (μεμίμηνται) the image of Christ, that is the conduct (πολιτείαν) and life in holiness (ἁγιασμῷ). For as image of the earthy one, that is Adam, we say is the life in disobedience (παρακοῇ) and sins, so also image of the heavenly, that is Christ, the holiness and the justification (δικαίωσιν) and the obedience (ὑπακοήν). As many therefore as were foreknown as going to be according to times (κατὰ καιρούς) conformed to and imitators (μιμηταί) of the life of Christ, according to what is possible (ἐγχωροῦν) for human nature, these also have been called. Those whom he foreordained, these also he called; and whom he called, these also he justified (ἐδικαίωσεν); whom he justified, these also he glorified (ἐδόξασεν). Nothing unlikely (ἀπεικός) that some make the matter a good starting-point (εὐάφορμον) of unbelief (ἀπιστίας), carried away (συνηρπασμένους) by ignorance (ἀμαθίας) and saying: if those whom he himself foreknew according to purpose and foreordained, these also have been called, nothing toward us who have not yet believed; for we have not been called, nor foreordained. To whom we will say that the one making the wedding (γάμους) for his son sent the servants (οἰκέτας) to gather the called (κεκλημένους), but they were not willing (ἤθελον) to come; but after those came in the called according to their own purpose (κατ' ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν), and thus the bridal hall (νυμφών) was filled with those reclining (ἀνακειμένων). Nothing therefore is seen lying as hindrance (ἐμποδών) to those willing to come; the foreknowledge (πρόγνωσις) wrongs (ἀδικεῖ) no one at all, nor indeed profits (ὀνίνησι) some. Since (ἐπεί) let them teach whether they too were not foreknown, those who by disobediences (ἀπειθείαις) insulted (ἐξυβρικότες) the God who called. But also some have been called and leapt into (εἰσπεπηδήκασι) the wedding, yet did not become chosen, nor were justified nor glorified; for what cause? that they were not clothed (ἠμφιέννυντο) in a robe (στολήν) befitting the wedding. Otherwise also we will find our Lord Jesus Christ himself having said openly (ἀναφανδόν): come to me all the toiling (κοπιῶντες) and burdened (πεφορτισμένοι), and I will give rest (ἀναπαύσω) to you. Behold, already he was calling all to himself; no one would be without share (ἀμοιρήσειε) of the grace upon being called; for in saying all, he makes absolutely (παντελῶς) no one sent away (ἀπόπεμπτον). What then shall we say to these? if God for us, who against us? who indeed did not spare (ἐφείσατο) his own Son. To those having chosen (ᾑρημένοις) to do good (ἀγαθοεργεῖν) all things work together, God shielding (ὑπερασπίζοντος); for the one having not spared (ἠφειδηκώς) the Son by nature (κατὰ φύσιν), that he might save those in danger (κινδυνεύοντας) and [continues in u07-rem-close].
pass_b_english: …me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). Yet in this matter one would not miss what is fitting if one said that some have been called according to purpose, both the purpose of the one who called them and their own. “For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed,” and so on (Romans 8:29). Many, he says, are called according to purpose, but not all are chosen (Matthew 22:14); only those have been honored who were also foreknown as those who would be conformed to the image of his Son.

What the image of his Son should be understood to be, the blessed Paul himself will make clear again, saying, “For just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one” (1 Corinthians 15:49). For those who have paid no heed to fleshly desires are the ones who have imitated the image of Christ, that is, the way of life and conduct that is in holiness. For just as we say that the image of the man of dust, that is, of Adam, is the life lived in disobedience and sins, so too the image of the heavenly one, that is, of Christ, is holiness, justification and obedience. All, then, who were foreknown as those who would, in their own times, be conformed to the life of Christ and be its imitators, so far as human nature allows, these have also been called. “And those whom he predestined he also called; and those whom he called he also justified; and those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:30).

It is not at all unlikely that some, carried away by ignorance, should make this matter a ready pretext for unbelief and say, “If those whom he foreknew according to purpose and predestined are the ones who have been called, it has nothing to do with us who have not yet believed; for we have not been called, nor have we been predestined.” To them we will say that the one who gave the wedding feast for his son sent his servants to gather those who had been called, but they would not come (Matthew 22:2–3). After them, those who were called according to their own purpose came in, and so the wedding hall was filled with guests (Matthew 22:10). So nothing is seen standing in the way of those who are willing to come. Foreknowledge does no wrong to anyone at all, nor does it give anyone an advantage. Otherwise, let them teach us whether those who in their disobedience outraged the God who called them were not foreknown as well. More than that, some were called and rushed into the wedding, yet they did not become chosen, nor were they justified or glorified. For what reason? Because they were not wearing a garment fit for the wedding (Matthew 22:11–12).

Besides, we shall find our Lord Jesus Christ himself saying openly, “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). See, he was already calling all people to himself, and no one would be without a share in the grace of being called; for in saying “all” he sends no one away at all. “What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son” (Romans 8:31–32). For those who have chosen to do good, all things work together, since God shields them. reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: Staged translation checked clause by clause; negations (οὐ μὴν ἅπαντες ἐκλεκτοί; ἀδικεῖ οὐδένα ... οὔτε ὀνίνησι), agency (the caller's and the called's purpose) and Scripture IDs (John 6:44; Romans 8:29, 8:30, 8:31–32; Matthew 22:2–3, 10, 11–12, 14; 1 Corinthians 15:49; Matthew 11:28) are right. Fixed in tr6.json: (1) 'It would be nothing unlikely for some ... to make' (stiff, and the Greek has no ἄν) now 'It is not at all unlikely that some ... should make'; (2) κατ' ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν was 'by their own purpose', now 'according to their own purpose' to keep Cyril's κατὰ πρόθεσιν thread; (3) stiff split clause 'whether those too were not foreknown who by their disobedience outraged...' reordered to 'whether those who in their disobedience outraged the God who called them were not foreknown as well'.
Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).

The row opens mid-quotation (με, ἐὰν μὴ ὁ Πατὴρ ... completes John 6:44 from u07-rem-early) and ends mid-sentence at ἵνα σώσῃ κινδυνεύοντας, καί; ἀπαλλάξῃ κινδύνων and the main clause follow in u07-rem-close. Ellipses mark both joins; nothing supplied.
τήν τε τοῦ κεκληκότος καὶ τὴν ἑαυτῶν: the feminine article picks up πρόθεσιν; rendered “both the purpose of the one who called them and their own”.
φησίν in “Many, he says, are called”: Cyril reports Paul's sense in words drawn from Matthew 22:14, not a quotation of Romans.
προορίζω rendered “predestine” throughout, the usual English for Romans 8:29–30.
τοὺς κεκλημένους in the parable rendered “those who had been called” (not “invited”) to keep Cyril's play on κλητοί / κέκληνται.
ἀδικεῖ δὲ οὐδένα τὸ σύμπαν ἡ πρόγνωσις, οὔτε μὴν ὀνίνησί τινας: foreknowledge neither harms nor helps; ὀνίνησι rendered “give anyone an advantage”, keeping the negation exact.
ἐπεὶ διδασκόντων: ἐπεί with a third-person imperative, “otherwise, let them teach us”; Cyril's point is that the disobedient were also foreknown, so foreknowledge did not cause their refusal.
τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ... Υἱοῦ: “the one who is his Son by nature”, keeping Cyril's term against adoptive sonship.
PG column numbers 221 and 222 and the page number 20 are dropped; the split word τού τους is read as τούτους.
